text: The biggest IPO in history just priced.
Anthropic sold shares at eighty-three dollars, above its range, raising about eighty-one billion.
That values it near one point five trillion.
Revenue grew about fourteen times in a year.
But the price is roughly forty-six times sales. You're paying for years of growth.
And the eighty billion dollar loss? Mostly a non-cash revaluation.
What about the P/E ratio? Officially, there isn't one. It lost money.
Using its best quarter, at eighty-three dollars you pay about three hundred eighty-five times profits. The S&P 500? About eighteen.
In plain English: at today's profits, it would take about three hundred eighty-five years to earn back the price.
To look like a normal stock, profits would need to grow more than twenty times.
Then it opened at eleven fifty Eastern: one hundred eleven dollars and fifty cents, up thirty-four percent from the IPO price.
At that price, Anthropic is worth about two trillion dollars.
The math changes too. Price-to-sales jumps to about sixty-two times.
And the P/E, from that best quarter and updated to the opening price, rises to about five hundred seventeen times.
Now profits would need to grow almost thirty times to look like a normal stock.
Day one is the headline. The numbers are the story.
So, is one hundred eleven dollars a share too much? What is Anthropic really worth? Tell us in the comments.
